solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Play Peter Pan director set up?

definitions.note: the question mark flags set up in the sense of framed

indicators.note: to play with something is to toy with it, so the letters that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A director wonders whether a production of Peter Pan has been rigged against them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like the stage show but signals rearranging PETERPAN into ENTRAPPE, before D is added. 'Set up' means framed or caught in a trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been framed or lured into a trap by a sting has been caught, the past participle sense.

clue.text: Faithful old wife heading to alimony court

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse

indicators.note: the heading, the very first letter, of the word alimony

parts.note: first letter gives A

explanation.surface: A loyal former wife is on her way to a divorce court to argue about maintenance payments.
explanation.definitionFit: A faithful copy or translation is precise and accurate, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Worked out and showered after shift's end

indicators.note: the showered part comes after the T, so this orders the charade
the end of shift is its final letter, which is picked here

parts.note: the possessive is just the word shift, whose end is wanted
rained, as in rained down on

explanation.surface: Someone exercised and then took a shower at the end of their working shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked out' reads as exercising, which fits the gym surface and the answer alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To have trained is to have exercised regularly to build fitness, the gym sense of worked out.

clue.text: Russian royal's port I polished off

indicators.note: polished off means finished or got rid of, so the letter I is removed from the port

parts.note: Alexandria is the great Egyptian port

explanation.surface: A Russian royal boasts of having devoured a whole glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' tempts as the drink; it is the Egyptian city. Take I out of ALEXANDRIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandra Feodorovna was the last Tsarina, wife of Nicholas II, so she was a royal of imperial Russia.

clue.text: Drug found in meal a captor cooked

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters have been prepared and mixed up into a new form

explanation.surface: A painkiller is discovered in food prepared by a kidnapper for a hostage.
explanation.definitionFit: Paracetamol is a common over-the-counter painkilling medicine, an example of a drug.

clue.text: I made a bloomer in party with husband

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration
H is the abbreviation for husband in genealogy and marriage records

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to a gaffe they committed at a party while with their husband.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is British slang for a blunder; the answer is the exclamation Homer Simpson makes after one.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is uttered on realising one has blundered, so it stands for an admission of a silly mistake.

clue.text: Some socks, a gumboot and cloak

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A list of wardrobe items: some socks, a rubber boot and a cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'and cloak' as the definition; 'and' is only a link word joining the hidden word to its meaning, so the definition is 'cloak'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sagum was the woollen military cloak worn by Roman soldiers, so it is a specific kind of cloak.

clue.text: Small old lady sent up pious Greek figure

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

indicators.note: in a down clue, sent up means read from the bottom upward

parts.note: old lady is slang for mother, MA
pi is informal British for pious or sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A slight elderly woman mocked a devout figure from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' looks like mockery but reverses MA in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sampi is an archaic letter of the Greek alphabet used as the numeral 900.

clue.text: Reportedly rubbish energy food from Italy

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard spoken, so the sound of the pieces is what counts

parts.note: to rubbish something is to knock it, criticise it; E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Supposedly a junk-food energy snack has come from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, KNOCK-E is close to the usual English pronunciation of the Italian dumplings.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnocchi are small Italian dumplings made from potato or semolina, a typical dish of that country.

clue.text: Be practicable to earn money in US, I'm told

indicators.note: I'm told means heard said, so what follows is how the words sound

parts.note: to make cents is to earn American money, the cent being a US coin

explanation.surface: Someone hears it is workable to make a living in America.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that makes sense is reasonable and workable, so the phrase means to be feasible or practical.

clue.text: A pal game to have a roll is not a pro

parts.note: a mate is a pal or friend

indicators.note: rolling over turns something back to front, so these letters reverse

parts.note: RU is rugby union, the game

explanation.surface: A friend's game involves a roll of the dice, which shows they aren't a professional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' is the sport rugby union, a standard crossword abbreviation, and the roll turns it back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur plays for love rather than payment, the opposite of a professional.

clue.text: Plant in border seen near Yale, perhaps

indicators.note: the second piece is placed beside the first

parts.note: a hem is the edge or border of a garment
Yale is a well-known brand of lock, hence perhaps

explanation.surface: A plant in a garden border is noticed close to Yale University.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yale' looks like the university but is the lock maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemlock is a poisonous flowering plant of the carrot family, famous for killing Socrates.

clue.text: State of fashion? God-awful primarily!

parts.note: ton is an old word for fashion, as in the bon ton

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letters of each part of the hyphenated word

explanation.surface: An exclamation about how dreadful the current trend in fashion is.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is an independent Pacific island kingdom, a sovereign country or nation.

clue.text: Pouches holding the king's crown jewels?

definitions.text: Pouches holding the king's crown jewels?

parts.words: Pouches holding the king's crown jewels?
parts.note: crown jewels is a jokey term for a man's genitals, and these Tudor garment pouches held them

explanation.walkthrough: The clue paints a royal treasury, but crown jewels here is slang for the male private parts, which a Tudor king covered with this garment flap.
explanation.definitionFit: These were pouched flaps on the front of men's breeches in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, as worn by Henry VIII.

clue.text: Awfully crude flag is thus?

indicators.note: awfully suggests the letters are badly treated and messed up into a new order

explanation.surface: A really vulgar banner is shameful, the clue suggests.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a crude flag would be shameful.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shameful brings disgrace and deserves condemnation, as an obscene banner would.

clue.text: Hat Slormgorm would put on student

indicators.note: the following piece is placed against the first, next to it

parts.note: L is a learner, as on a British L-plate
the setter Slormgorm would say I'd, I would

explanation.surface: A hat that the setter would place on a student's head.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves by name, so Slormgorm would is I'D; L for learner gives the student.
explanation.definitionFit: Lid is informal slang for a hat or cap, the covering on top of the head.

clue.text: I travel to Barking to see David Blaine?

definitions.note: the illusionist is an example, hence the question mark

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters are deranged and reordered

explanation.surface: Someone travels to Barking, east London, to watch the magician David Blaine.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of London, but here it is British slang for crazy, signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The illusionist David Blaine is famous for stunts in which he appears to float above the ground.

clue.text: Hate drug stop led by detective

indicators.note: the detective comes first and leads the rest

parts.note: E is ecstasy, the drug
a station is a stop on a train line

explanation.surface: A detective spearheads a hated drug bust.
explanation.definitionFit: Detestation is intense loathing, a strong synonym for hate used as a noun.

clue.text: Early bus exploding by YMCA … duck!

indicators.note: exploding blows the letters apart so they land in a new order

parts.note: Y is a common short name for the YMCA

explanation.surface: A bus bursts into flames near the YMCA and someone shouts to take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duck!' looks like a command to take cover; it is the bird. Aylesbury is a town in Buckinghamshire, England, that gave its name to a breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aylesbury is a white English breed of domestic duck raised for meat.

clue.text: Officer dim cavalier got in a lather

indicators.note: getting in a lather means getting agitated, so the letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: A dim-witted, careless officer becomes flustered.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice admiral is a senior naval rank below admiral, so the holder is a commissioned officer.

clue.text: Mild Labour leader gets in fix

indicators.note: the letter enters the other word, so one goes inside the other

parts.note: to cement something is to fix it firmly

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A gentle head of the Labour Party finds himself in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' suggests a politician such as Clement Attlee, but it is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement weather is mild and pleasant, and a clement judge is lenient, so both mean gentle.

clue.text: Signal gadget man picked up

indicators.note: picked up means heard, so what counts is how the letter sounds

parts.note: Q is the gadget-maker in the James Bond films

explanation.surface: A device enthusiast hears a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is a prompt or signal telling an actor or performer to begin.

clue.text: Income dictates housing? Laughable!

indicators.note: housing means holding within, so the answer is inside these words

explanation.surface: It is ridiculous that what you earn decides where you can live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'housing' reads as accommodation but signals the answer held within the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something comedic is funny or comic, so it provokes laughter.

clue.text: People in general belch it up, sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Members of society, unfortunately, burp and bring it back up.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase denotes ordinary citizens collectively, the community at large.

clue.text: Range of unpopular lavatories?

indicators.note: unpopular reads as un-popular: in means popular, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: urinals are lavatories for men

explanation.surface: A selection of public toilets nobody likes to use.
explanation.walkthrough: IN means popular, so 'unpopular' asks for URINALS without IN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Urals are a mountain chain dividing Europe from Asia in Russia.

clue.text: Dance held in Assam ballroom

indicators.note: held in means contained within, so the answer sits inside these words

explanation.surface: A dance takes place in a ballroom in Assam, India.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is a lively Brazilian ballroom and carnival dance.

clue.text: A never-ending environmental grant

indicators.note: the word does not reach its end, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: green means environmentally friendly

explanation.surface: An unending ecological subsidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grant' looks like a noun for a subsidy but is the verb meaning concede.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant a point is to concede or accept it, the same as going along with it.

clue.text: Will article by lawyers ultimately stand?

parts.note: the is the definite article
the bar is the legal profession of barristers

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of stand

explanation.surface: A question about whether a legal document drafted by lawyers will hold up in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a legal testament; it is Shakespeare's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: William Shakespeare is called by this nickname, the great poet of Stratford.

clue.text: Call friend in America up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from the bottom

parts.note: bud is American slang for a friend

explanation.surface: Phoning a pal across the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: To dub someone is to name or give them a title, as when knighting.

clue.text: One who started a company in fall

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the person who establishes a business
second meaning: to collapse or sink, as a ship or plan does

explanation.surface: A company's originator is in decline.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names an establishing person, while the verb means to fail or sink, as a ship that goes down.

clue.text: Informers taking in English judges

indicators.note: the outer word takes the other inside it

parts.note: a rat is slang for an informer

explanation.surface: Police informers are taking in English judges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'judges' looks like a noun for court officials; it is the verb meaning assesses.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate something is to assess or evaluate it, so rates means assesses.

clue.text: Corporate complaint?

parts.note: corporate here means relating to the body, so this is a bodily ailment that also means a grumble

explanation.walkthrough: Corporate seems to concern a business, but it comes from the Latin for body, so a corporate complaint is a stomach pain.
explanation.definitionFit: A stomach pain is an ailment of the abdomen, and informally the word also means a whinge or grumble.
